headings.text: Different perspectives on the digital revolutions
Technology and society: three examples, three lessons
Example 1: Bicycles, or how social factors shape technology
Example 2: Automobile, or how technologies develop with their environments
Example 3: Ships, or how technologies often stick around longer than we think

html:
The big picture

The usual story of technology is a march of inventions that then change society. This unit replaces it with a two-way relationship, using three historical examples. Bicycles show that social groups shape technology: early designs meant different things to different users (interpretative flexibility), and one design won only when the problem itself was redefined (closure). Cars show that technologies develop together with their environment: they need physical and regulatory infrastructures, and once those exist they create path dependencies and lock-in. Ships show that old technologies stick around and get adapted (technology-in-use, creole technologies), which is why maintenance matters as much as innovation. The conclusion is Bijker's sociotechnical ensemble: neither technology nor society determines the other; both are built together. For robotics & AI this means asking not only what is new, but who gives it meaning, what infrastructure and work keep it running, and how it fits into what already exists.

In today's class

  • Which lessons to draw from Ada Lovelace's early ideas of AI?
  • Technology and society: three examples, three lessons
  • Maintenance in robotics & AI
  • Some resources at AAU

Different perspectives on the digital revolutions

Slide image: a portrait of Ada Lovelace.

  • Different 'camps' around the question: can machines think?
  • Computer revolution v. AI revolution
  • Essential issue: to improve human lives
Connection

This slide summarises the Isaacson reading (Class 02 – The bigger picture): the Turing camp expects machines to match and surpass human intelligence (the "AI revolution"), the Lovelace camp sees computers as tools that extend human creativity and judgement (the "computer revolution", human–machine symbiosis). Isaacson's point, and the slide's last bullet: the deciding question is not whether machines can think but what for, namely improving human lives.

Technology and society: three examples, three lessons

Example 1: Bicycles, or how social factors shape technology

Slide images: a high-wheeled "penny-farthing" bicycle and a later bicycle with two equal wheels.

  • How to explain these weird-looking old bicycles with uneven wheels?
  • They served different purposes → the interpretation (meaning) of a single technical artefact can be flexible.
  • Bicycles as fast & skill-based, or as dangerous and inappropriate machines?
  • Variation and selection: different meanings lead to different designs.
  • Why does one design (often) persist, and not others?
  • Closure: reinterpretation of the problem / redefining a technology's meaning.
  • The rubber air tyre on the bicycle: both safe and fast!
Intuition — interpretative flexibility and closure

This is the classic case of the social construction of technology (SCOT, Pinch & Bijker). The high-wheeler had a huge front wheel because the pedals drove it directly: a bigger wheel meant more distance per pedal turn, so more speed. For young sporting men it was a thrilling machine that showed off skill; for women, older people and cautious riders it was a dangerous one that threw riders over the handlebars. Same object, different meanings: that's interpretative flexibility, and each relevant social group pushed for a different design (variation). Closure came with the air tyre: introduced to dampen vibration (a comfort and safety fix), it then won races, so the "safe" low bicycle with air tyres became the "fast" one too. The conflict wasn't settled by finding the technically best design, but by the problem being redefined until one design satisfied both groups.

Common mistake — "the best design simply won"

Tempting: the safety bicycle replaced the high-wheeler because it was technically superior. But "superior" depends on what you want: for the sporting group, the high-wheeler was the better machine, and the air tyre was at first mocked as an ugly comfort gadget. Which design counts as "working" is decided by the groups using it. The same applies to robots: whether a care robot "works" depends on whether you ask the hospital manager, the nurse or the patient.

Example 2: Automobile, or how technologies develop with their environments

Slide images: the Flintstones' foot-powered car, and a traffic jam on a multi-lane road.

  • What is needed for cars to function as a mode of transportation?
  • Physical infrastructures: roads, gas stations, parking places, …
  • Social/regulatory infrastructures: rules of the road (right of way, (mostly) maximum speed, …)
  • Not only enabling cars to drive, but creating entire worlds with them.
  • Path dependencies, lock-in effects and social spill-overs.
  • "No alternative to automobility" (is a choice).
  • Infrastructures (e.g. for electric 'fuelling') not in place.
  • Social meaning of technology / resistance to change ("autonomy").
Intuition — path dependency and lock-in

Path dependency: early choices shape which later choices are easy. Once cities, suburbs, shopping centres and jobs are built around roads, life without a car becomes hard, so people buy cars, which justifies more roads. Lock-in: the system then resists change even when a better alternative exists, because everything around it is adapted to the old technology. Electric cars face exactly this: the car itself is ready, but the charging infrastructure, habits and regulations grew up around petrol. And cars carry social meaning ("freedom", "autonomy"), which is why "there is no alternative" is a choice society keeps making, not a law of nature.

Example 3: Ships, or how technologies often stick around longer than we think

Slide images: a cruise ship, and a Thai long-tail boat.

  • Despite innovation, incumbent technologies often remain in use for a long time.
  • Technologies may also change meaning and be used for different purposes (e.g. cruise ships).
  • Single things' lifespan is extended through maintenance and retro-fitting.
  • Technology use may differ across groups; it may be adjusted to specific needs ("creole technologies").
  • Technology also has a cultural value/significance.
  • Focus not only on innovation, but on technology-in-use.
Intuition — technology-in-use and creole technologies

Histories of technology usually stop at the invention. The historian David Edgerton (The Shock of the Old) argues for looking at technology-in-use: which technologies people actually rely on, and these are mostly old ones. Ships are his kind of example: passenger liners lost their transport role to aeroplanes and came back as cruise ships, a new meaning for an old technology. Creole technologies are technologies adapted locally, often in poorer regions, into something their inventors never planned: the long-tail boat in the picture is a traditional boat driven by a car or truck engine on a long propeller shaft.

In conclusion: sociotechnical ensembles

Slide image: a photo of Wiebe Bijker.

"Instead of technical artifacts, our unit of analysis is now the 'sociotechnical ensemble' […] 'Society is not determined by technology, nor is technology determined by society. Both emerge as two sides of the sociotechnical coin during the construction processes of artifacts, facts, and relevant social groups.'" — Wiebe Bijker, Of Bicycles, Bakelites, and Bulbs, p. 274

Common mistake — technological determinism

The everyday view is technological determinism: technology develops by its own logic and then "impacts" society ("AI will change everything"). The opposite error is pure social determinism: society simply decides what technology becomes. The three examples show neither works alone. The bicycle's design was shaped by social groups, but the car, once built into cities, shaped how people live. A sociotechnical ensemble treats the artefact, its users, its infrastructure and its rules as one system that changes together.

Worked example — the three lessons applied to a robot

Take an autonomous delivery robot on city pavements.

  1. Social factors shape it (bicycle): who are the relevant social groups, and what does the robot mean to each? The company: cheap last-mile delivery. Pedestrians and wheelchair users: an obstacle on the pavement. The city: a regulatory problem. Its design (size, speed, where it may drive) will be negotiated among these meanings.
  2. It develops with its environment (car): it needs kerb ramps, mapped routes, charging, mobile networks and rules (may it use the pavement? who is liable for a collision?). Once cities adapt to it, that creates path dependencies of its own.
  3. It meets old technology (ships): it competes with cargo bikes and couriers that are cheap, flexible and maintained by people who know them, and after the launch someone has to clean sensors, repair wheels and recover stuck robots.

Deciding question: for any "new" robot or AI system, ask who gives it meaning, what has to exist around it, and who keeps it running.

"Maintenance" in robotics and AI

Slide image: a toy robot holding a wrench.

  • How can we think about robotics/AI "after innovation"?

    • Technology as more than just innovation ("in use")
    • What is the role of basic infrastructure?
    • What is the work involved? Especially maintenance?
  • What do you think answers to these questions tell us about 'the new' in relation to robotics and AI?
Connection

This is the Russell & Vinsel reading (Class 02 – The bigger picture): innovation is overvalued, while maintenance, repair and infrastructure, and the often invisible labour behind them, keep technology working. For AI the maintenance work is easy to overlook: updating models as the world changes, labelling and cleaning data, monitoring for errors and bias, keeping servers and power running. Class 4 (Class 04 – Human and environmental costs) picks up the human and environmental side of that work.

Literature for the lecture

  • Bijker, Wiebe (1995): Of bicycles, bakelites and bulbs. Towards a theory of sociotechnical change. Cambridge: The MIT Press.
  • Edgerton, David: The shock of the old. Technology and global history since 1900. London: Profile Books.
  • Nye, David (2006): Technology matters. Questions to live with. Cambridge: The MIT Press.
  • Peters, Peter (2006): Time, innovation and mobilities: Travel in technological cultures. London: Taylor & Francis.

Terms

  • Interpretative flexibility — one artefact can mean different things to different social groups (the high-wheeler as sports machine or as danger).
  • Relevant social group — a group that shares a meaning of an artefact and influences its development (sporting riders, women cyclists, …).
  • Closure — the point where the controversy about a technology ends, often by redefining the problem rather than by one side "winning".
  • Infrastructure (physical, regulatory) — what has to exist around a technology for it to function: roads and fuel stations; traffic rules.
  • Path dependency — earlier decisions constrain later options.
  • Lock-in — a system stays with a technology because everything around it is adapted to it, even when alternatives exist.
  • Technology-in-use — studying the technologies people actually use, mostly old ones, rather than only inventions (Edgerton).
  • Creole technology — a technology adapted locally to new uses and needs, often outside its place of origin.
  • Maintenance / retro-fitting — the work of keeping existing technology running and updating it, extending its life.
  • Sociotechnical ensemble — technology and society treated as one co-evolving unit; neither determines the other (Bijker).
  • Technological determinism — the view (criticised here) that technology develops on its own and then drives social change.
